Some other proposed superordinate objectives

Criticality: The Entropic Brain

A growing body of work suggests that the brain does not merely optimize what it computes but also the dynamical regime in which it computes, self-tuning toward a narrow operating point–criticality–at the boundary between ordered (low-entropy, rigid, highly predictable) and disordered (high-entropy, labile, noise-dominated) dynamics. Criticality, borrowed from statistical physics, refers to the phase transition between these regimes: a system poised at this edge exhibits spatiotemporal activity patterns that follow power-law (scale-free) statistics rather than the characteristic scales expected of either phase alone. The landmark observation of neuronal avalanches–cascades of spiking activity whose sizes and durations follow power-law distributions with exponents matching those predicted by critical branching processes–provided the first direct cortical evidence for near-critical dynamics in vitro and subsequently in vivo 1, 2. Complementary signatures at larger scales include long-range temporal correlations and 1/f1/f-like spectral structure in EEG/MEG and fMRI signals 3, 4, scale-free functional connectivity fluctuations, and maximal dynamic range and susceptibility of cortical populations near the critical point 5, 6. The avalanche analysis illustrates the empirical signature discussed here (Figure).

Why would this matter as a candidate superordinate objective? The theoretical motivation is that criticality simultaneously optimizes a constellation of information-processing desiderata: maximal dynamic range (the range of input intensities a network can discriminate is maximized at criticality, because the network is sensitive enough to amplify weak signals without saturating on strong ones) 5, maximal information transmission and storage (mutual information between inputs and outputs peaks at the critical point, as do measures of information capacity) 6, 7, maximal computational flexibility (the repertoire of distinguishable network states–and transitions among them–is largest at criticality, enabling the system to rapidly reconfigure for diverse tasks without requiring structural rewiring) 8, 9, and optimal balance between integration and segregation (critical networks support both local specialized processing and long-range coordination, precisely the regime needed for hierarchical generative modeling) 6. In the language of the preceding sections, criticality can be understood as the dynamical regime that jointly supports the objectives already discussed: compression progress is fastest when the network’s representational repertoire is maximal (criticality maximizes the number of distinguishable activity patterns available for encoding); empowerment is highest when the system can flexibly generate many distinct output trajectories; and EFE minimization is most effective when the generative model can both propagate precise predictions (requiring some order) and remain responsive to surprising evidence (requiring some disorder). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

The entropic brain hypothesis 10, 11 synthesizes these observations into a unifying framework, proposing that the quality of conscious states can be placed on an axis of neural entropy (closely related to criticality), with the ordinary waking state representing a near-critical regime that has been finely tuned by evolution, development, and moment-to-moment neuromodulatory regulation. Deviations toward subcriticality (excessive order)–associated with reduced entropy, stereotyped dynamics, and over-weighted priors–are linked to psychopathologies of rigidity such as depression, addiction, OCD, and anorexia, where behavior and cognition become trapped in narrow, self-reinforcing attractors 11. Deviations toward supercriticality (excessive disorder)–associated with elevated entropy, weakened top-down constraints, and flattened priors–characterize psychedelic states, early psychosis, and certain acute stress responses, where the model "loosens" and normally suppressed hypotheses flood awareness 12, 10, 13. This is more than analogy: serotonergic psychedelics (which agonize cortical 5-HT2A_{2A} receptors concentrated in layer V pyramidal neurons) measurably increase neural signal entropy, reduce the strength of top-down predictions, and flatten the precision hierarchy–temporarily pushing cortical dynamics toward supercriticality and producing subjective loosening of prior beliefs that can, under controlled conditions, enable therapeutic "model revision" in previously rigid psychopathological states 13, 14, 15. The proposed entropy–cognition relationship is summarized in the source schematic (Figure). The functional-network comparison makes the proposed change in integration concrete (Figure). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Mechanistically, the brain appears to maintain proximity to criticality via homeostatic tuning of the excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance: cortical circuits actively regulate synaptic strengths, intrinsic excitability, and inhibitory gain to keep network dynamics near the critical point, recovering from perturbations on timescales of minutes to hours 16, 17, 18. Neuromodulatory systems–particularly tonic serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine, and acetylcholine–act as global criticality regulators, shifting the operating point along the order-disorder axis by modulating E/I ratio, gain, and precision weighting across cortex 14, 11, 19. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

An important caveat: while the theoretical case for criticality as an organizing principle is compelling, empirical claims remain debated. Power-law distributions are notoriously difficult to distinguish from alternative heavy-tailed distributions with finite data 20, the brain may operate slightly subcritically rather than exactly at the critical point (which would offer robustness against runaway excitation while retaining most computational benefits) 21, and the relationship between mesoscale neural criticality and the macroscale "entropic brain" measures remains to be fully bridged 9. Criticality did not receive a full subsection here because it is arguably better understood as an emergent consequence of the superordinate objectives already treated–a dynamical-regime property that results from optimizing compression, empowerment, and flexible inference under metabolic constraints–rather than an independent objective with its own dedicated motivational circuitry. The brain does not "seek criticality" the way it seeks food or social inclusion; rather, critical dynamics are what you get when a metabolically constrained, hierarchical, precision-weighted generative model is well-tuned for the joint optimization described in the preceding sections.

Resonance Maximization: The Brain as a Coupled Oscillator

An alternative–and arguably deeper–way to state what the brain "wants" is that it seeks to become structurally isomorphic to the causal architecture of its environment: to mirror, in its internal connectivity and dynamics, the statistical and causal regularities of the world it must predict and control. This idea has roots in cybernetics (Ashby’s Law of Requisite Variety: a controller must have at least as much internal variety as the system it regulates 22), in Conant and Ashby’s Good Regulator Theorem (every good regulator of a system must be–or contain–a model of that system 23), and in the free-energy principle’s implication that a system that persists in exchanging signals with its environment will, over time, come to mirror the statistical structure of that environment in its internal states 24, 25. The resulting framework treats the brain not as an input-output device that happens to predict well, but as a coupled dynamical system whose internal structure is progressively sculpted–by evolution, development, and learning–until its state-space geometry resonates with (i.e., is homeomorphic to) the causal manifold of its ecological niche. "Resonance" here is not merely metaphorical: when two dynamical systems are coupled and one comes to mirror the other’s attractor landscape, they exhibit generalized synchronization–the internal trajectory of the "model" system becomes a smooth, invertible function of the "target" system’s trajectory–meaning that the model’s states reliably track (and can be decoded into) the target’s states with minimal lag and error 26, 27. In information-theoretic terms, resonance corresponds to maximizing the mutual information I(Sbrain;Senv)I(S_{\text{brain}}; S_{\text{env}}) between internal and environmental state trajectories, subject to a complexity/capacity constraint on the internal model–precisely the rate-distortion tradeoff that compression-based accounts formalize 28. In dynamical-systems terms, it corresponds to the brain’s attractor landscape acquiring the same topological structure (number, type, and connectivity of attractors and saddle connections) as the environment’s latent causal dynamics, so that transitions in the world map onto corresponding transitions in the brain with preserved adjacency and direction 23, 25.

Several lines of evidence support the claim that the brain converges toward structural isomorphism with environmental dynamics rather than merely learning input-output mappings. Neural representational geometry increasingly mirrors task and stimulus geometry: in trained animals and humans, the population-level geometry of neural activity in relevant cortical areas (measured via representational similarity analysis or manifold-learning techniques) comes to reflect the metric and topological structure of the stimulus or task space–e.g., the ring topology of head-direction cells mirrors the rotational symmetry of heading 29, grid-cell lattices mirror the translational symmetry of Euclidean space 30, tonotopic and retinotopic maps preserve the neighbourhood structure of frequency and visual space, and object-category representations in inferotemporal cortex arrange along axes that mirror ecological similarity rather than arbitrary labeling 31, 32. More strikingly, hippocampal and entorhinal "cognitive maps" generalize spatial coding motifs to abstract relational structures: grid-like hexagonal coding has been observed during navigation of conceptual spaces parameterized by non-spatial stimulus dimensions 33, 34, and hippocampal representations of social hierarchies and abstract task graphs exhibit geometric structure that mirrors the latent relational topology 35, 36, 37. These findings suggest that the brain does not merely learn what predicts what (a correlation structure) but installs internal dynamics whose geometry and topology recapitulate the causal/relational geometry of the domain–a stronger condition than predictive accuracy alone. At the network level, the hierarchical laminar architecture of cortex (with distinct feedforward, lateral, and feedback connection classes) can be interpreted as an architectural prior that makes it efficient to mirror hierarchically structured generative processes in the world: the factorized, layered connectivity of the cortical sheet is itself a structural "pre-resonance" with the compositional, multi-scale causal structure of natural environments 38, 39. Representational geometry is illustrated by activity spaces and their distance matrices (Figure). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

The resonance view clarifies a feature of neural coding that is otherwise puzzling: why the brain appears to invest heavily in preserving relational and geometric structure in its representations rather than adopting maximally compressed, but geometrically arbitrary, codes. A lookup table or hash function could in principle achieve zero prediction error with no structural resemblance to the environment, but such representations would fail catastrophically under distribution shift, novel recombination, or transfer–precisely the conditions that biological agents face continuously. Representations that are structurally isomorphic to environmental dynamics support zero-shot generalization: if the internal geometry mirrors the external causal geometry, then novel inputs that occupy unexplored regions of the environmental manifold will map onto the correct region of internal state space by geometric interpolation, without requiring new training data 32, 40. This is the representational analogue of the good-regulator theorem’s implication: a structurally isomorphic model is not merely accurate on trained data but robust and compositionally generalizable, because new situations are handled by the same structural relationships that governed old ones. Viewed this way, the compression objective described in the "Intrinsic Motivation" subsection and the resonance objective are not competing accounts but two faces of the same imperative: compression seeks to minimize description length, which (for structured environments) is achieved precisely by discovering and internalizing the causal factors and symmetries of the data-generating process–i.e., by becoming isomorphic to it 41, 42. Empowerment, similarly, is maximized when the agent’s internal model accurately mirrors the controllable degrees of freedom of the environment, because only a veridical causal model supports reliable action-outcome differentiation across the full action space. The symmetry-based comparison connects biological and artificial representations (Figure).

This framework was not given a full subsection because, like criticality, resonance maximization is arguably not an independent objective with dedicated motivational circuitry but rather the representational endpoint that the brain converges toward when it successfully minimizes free energy, maximizes compression progress, and expands empowerment in a structured world. The good-regulator theorem guarantees that a system coupled to an environment and minimizing prediction error over sufficient time will come to mirror that environment’s structure–making isomorphism a consequence of the objectives already treated rather than a separate drive. Nevertheless, the resonance framing adds explanatory value that pure prediction-error or compression language sometimes obscures: it foregrounds geometric and topological fidelity as the relevant notion of model quality (not just scalar loss reduction), it explains why the brain preserves structure that is "wasteful" from a pure minimum-code-length standpoint but essential for robustness and transfer, and it connects neural representation learning to deep results in dynamical systems theory and cybernetics that ground the entire enterprise of biological modeling in physically principled terms 23, 25, 24.

Neural Darwinism: Goal-Directed Agents All the Way Down

A recurring motif in the preceding sections is that the brain’s global objectives (compression, empowerment, EFE minimization) are realized not by a central optimizer issuing commands but by distributed, competing, locally goal-directed elements–neurons, synapses, neural groups, cortical columns, large-scale networks–whose interactions produce globally adaptive behavior as an emergent population-level outcome rather than a top-down design. This perspective finds its most explicit formulation in Edelman’s Neural Darwinism (the Theory of Neuronal Group Selection, TNGS), which proposes that the brain implements a genuinely selectionist process–variation, competition, differential amplification–operating over populations of neuronal groups, analogous in logical structure (though not mechanism) to natural selection over organisms 43, 44. TNGS identifies three stages: (i) developmental selection, in which genetically guided but stochastic processes (axon pathfinding, dendritic arborization, activity-dependent refinement) generate a vast, partially random primary repertoire of neuronal groups with diverse connectivity patterns–an anatomical "population" over which selection can act 43, 45; (ii) experiential selection, in which postnatal experience differentially strengthens or weakens synaptic populations via Hebbian and reward-modulated plasticity, amplifying groups whose response properties are functionally useful and allowing others to atrophy–producing a secondary repertoire adapted to the organism’s actual environment 43, 44; and (iii) reentrant signaling, in which reciprocal connections among selected groups create synchronized, mutually reinforcing ensembles that bind distributed features into coherent percepts and action plans–the mechanism by which local "winners" of selection are integrated into globally coherent function 44. Critically, this framework was paralleled and in some respects anticipated by Changeux’s selective stabilization theory, which proposed that an initial exuberance of synaptic connections is pruned by activity-dependent competition: synapses that participate in functional circuits are stabilized while redundant or non-functional ones are eliminated, implementing a Darwinian logic at the synaptic population level 45, 46. The empirical reality of this overproduction-and-pruning dynamic is now well established: human cortex overproduces synapses by roughly 50% during early postnatal life and then selectively eliminates them through adolescence in a region- and layer-specific maturational sequence 47, 48, and this pruning is not random but activity-shaped–a selection process whose "fitness criterion" is functional participation in viable circuits. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

The deeper theoretical insight–and the reason for the subtitle "goal-directed agents all the way down"–is that selectionist logic is not confined to neurons or synapses but operates at every spatial and temporal scale of neural organization, producing a nested hierarchy of competent agents each pursuing local objectives whose alignment produces (but does not guarantee) globally adaptive behavior. At the molecular/synaptic scale, individual synapses can be modeled as autonomous reinforcement learners that adjust their own transmission probability to maximize a local reward signal (postsynaptic depolarization, neuromodulatory reinforcement, retrograde signaling): Seung’s formalization shows that stochastic synaptic transmission combined with a global success signal is sufficient for individual synapses to implement a REINFORCE-like policy gradient, converging on transmission policies that maximize reward without any synapse "knowing" the network’s global objective 49. Loewenstein and Seung extended this to show that Hebbian synapses performing operant matching–distributing synaptic resources in proportion to experienced reinforcement rates–behave optimally under assumptions analogous to foraging theory, treating synaptic "weight" as a depletable resource allocated competitively among afferents 50. At the neuronal scale, individual neurons compete for metabolic resources, trophic factors (the classical neurotrophic hypothesis: target-derived NGF/BDNF is produced in limited quantities, and only neurons that secure sufficient trophic support survive developmental apoptosis 51, 52), and representational territory: cortical map expansion following increased use of a body part or sensory modality reflects competitive Hebbian displacement at the population level, with "winning" neurons literally expanding their receptive fields at the expense of less-active neighbours 53, 54. At the assembly/group scale, Calvin’s "cerebral code" hypothesis and related Darwinian neurodynamics proposals argue that spatiotemporal firing patterns (cell assemblies, synfire chains, cortical hexagonal mosaics) compete for replication across cortical territory in a process isomorphic to clonal selection: a pattern that "works" (generates accurate predictions, drives successful actions, receives neuromodulatory reinforcement) is copied to adjacent cortical columns via lateral excitatory connections, while patterns that fail are overwritten–implementing a rapid, intra-lifetime "evolution" of neural codes on timescales of hundreds of milliseconds 55, 56. At the network/coalition scale, global workspace and ignition models treat large-scale conscious access as the outcome of competition among neuronal coalitions: multiple assemblies vie for entry into a capacity-limited prefrontal-parietal workspace, and the "winning" coalition suppresses competitors via lateral inhibition, broadcasts its content globally, and thereby shapes downstream processing and memory consolidation 57, 58. The "goal" of each coalition is local (sustain its own coherent activation), but the competitive dynamic ensures that only the most contextually relevant coalition achieves global influence–a selectionist mechanism for attentional prioritization. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

A powerful modern generalization of this multi-scale selectionist view comes from Levin’s multi-scale competency architecture, which argues that goal-directed problem-solving is not a property that emerges only at the level of whole-brain neural computation but is a scale-free property exhibited by biological systems at every level of organization–from ion channels and individual cells through tissues, organs, and organisms to swarms and societies 59, 60. Individual cells navigate transcriptional, metabolic, and morphogenetic spaces using local signaling and bioelectric gradients; cell collectives solve anatomical problems (regenerating limbs, correcting developmental perturbations) by coordinating toward target morphologies encoded in bioelectric pattern memories; and neural networks implement the cognitive competencies discussed throughout this document–each level constituting an agent with its own "cognitive lightcone" (the space of states it can sense, represent, and act upon) that is nested within and partially controlled by agents at higher and lower scales 61. This multi-scale agency perspective reframes the brain not as a single optimizer but as a society of nested optimizers–a coalition of goal-directed subsystems at every spatial grain from single synapses to whole-brain networks–whose alignment is mediated by the architectural priors (shared neuromodulatory broadcasts, hierarchical connectivity, common metabolic constraints) that evolution installed to ensure that local competitions produce globally coherent behavior. Czegel, Szathmary, and colleagues formalize one key linkage, showing that replicator populations (competing, differentially amplified entities at any scale) performing selection naturally implement Bayesian inference: the population distribution over variants converges toward the posterior distribution over hypotheses given data, with fitness playing the role of likelihood 62. This result provides a principled bridge between the selectionist and inferential framings: Neural Darwinism and predictive processing / active inference are not competing theories but dual descriptions of the same underlying dynamic–selection is inference, performed by populations of competing elements whose differential survival embodies belief updating. The proposed scaling of cognitive boundaries is depicted schematically (Figure).

This framework did not receive its own subsection because, at the level of global brain objectives, Neural Darwinism and multi-scale competency are best understood as accounts of the implementation mechanism–how the brain realizes compression, empowerment, and EFE minimization–rather than as independent objectives. No neuron "wants" to minimize whole-organism free energy; it "wants" (in a minimal, non-sentient sense) to secure trophic support, maintain its membrane potential, and strengthen synapses that predict its inputs. But the nested competitive architecture ensures that these local wants, filtered through genetically installed connectivity priors and shaped by neuromodulatory reinforcement that reflects organism-level outcomes, collectively approximate the global objectives treated above–much as firms pursuing profit in a well-regulated market can collectively approximate efficient resource allocation without any firm representing the social welfare function. The selectionist framing nonetheless adds explanatory value that pure top-down optimization language misses: it explains why neural representations are diverse and redundant (variation is the fuel of selection), why pruning and competition are as important as growth (selection requires elimination), why neuromodulatory broadcast is so architecturally central (it is the "fitness signal" that aligns local competitions with global objectives), and why the brain is so robust to damage (a selectionist system degrades gracefully because surviving elements can be re-selected for new roles 43, 54)–properties that are natural consequences of a Darwinian architecture but require special explanation under a centralized-optimizer view.
